title: "Tokenisation Is Not in APX: Every Tokenizer You Ship Is a Heuristic"

categories:

summary: "A complexity-theory result from Cambridge proves no polynomial-time algorithm can approximate optimal tokenization within any constant factor - which reframes BPE and UnigramLM as pragmatic heuristics rather than near-optimal solutions."
image: "/assets/post-images/2026-11-26-tokenisation-not-in-apx.svg"
---

Every large language model starts with a choice that almost nobody defends: how to cut text into tokens. **BPE** merges the most frequent adjacent pair, greedily, until a vocabulary budget is exhausted. **UnigramLM** fits a latent segmentation with expectation-maximisation against a unigram likelihood. Both are treated as if they were engineering conveniences approximating some optimum. A new complexity result from **Violeta Kastreva, Philip Whittington, Dennis Komm and Tiago Pimentel** says the premise is wrong.

Their claim is precise and, in a way, worse than "tokenization is hard". They prove that unless P=NP, **no polynomial-time algorithm can find a tokenizer whose objective is within any constant factor of the optimum** - which is the formal statement that **tokenisation is not in the APX complexity class**. APX-hardness means that for some constant c>1, no efficient algorithm can guarantee a solution within factor c of optimal; "not in APX" means no approximation scheme at all, for any constant factor. The results hold for **direct tokenisation** (segment each string optimally from scratch) and **bottom-up tokenisation** (merge-based, i.e. BPE-style), under both a **compression objective** and a **unigram log-likelihood objective**, over binary or larger alphabets. They go further: even over a **unary alphabet**, direct tokenisation is APX-hard.

The prior literature had been close but not complete - **Kozma and Voderholzer (2026)** showed bottom-up tokenisation is APX-hard, and **Lim et al. (2025)** showed direct tokenisation is NP-hard. This paper closes the gap and shows there is no approximation guarantee to be had in the general case.

What it means practically is blunt. The reductions leave open only approximation guarantees close in ratio to **character-level tokenisation** - that is, the trivial baseline. Any meaningful guarantee about how good a tokenizer is must be **dataset-specific**, and the authors' own limitation section concedes the hardness constructions are unlike natural text, where current algorithms may sit near the optimum. Their proposed next step is not a better algorithm but a **certificate**: proving how close a tokenizer is to optimal on a given target corpus, with LP-based work (Tempus et al., 2026) as a first step.

So the practical takeaway is not "use a different tokenizer". It is that the tokenizer you ship is a heuristic whose quality on your corpus is unverified, and that BPE's known bad worst-case compression behaviour is not an implementation artefact but a structural consequence. Tokenizer training, quietly, is the one part of the LLM stack that nobody can promise to get right.

Source: [arXiv:2611.34938 - Tokenisation is not in APX](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.34938)
